CausalChain: Fasting -> alteration in ncRNA expression (upregulation of tumor-suppressive miRNAs, e.g., miR-34a) -> downregulation of HK2 -> decreased aerobic glycolysis and lactate production -> reduced acidification of tumor microenvironment -> diminished immune evasion -> increased chemosensitivity (e.g., to sorafenib)
Hypothesis: Intermittent fasting reprograms the noncoding RNA profile in HCC, leading to suppressed HK2-driven aerobic glycolysis, reduction in lactate-mediated immunosuppression, and enhanced sensitivity to chemotherapeutic agents such as sorafenib.
Abstract: Recent studies on hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) underscore the critical role of aerobic glycolysis in supporting tumor proliferation, metastasis, and drug resistance. Building on these insights, we propose that intermittent fasting induces a shift in the noncoding RNA (ncRNA) landscape, which in turn suppresses key glycolytic enzymes such as hexokinase 2 (HK2). This ncRNA-mediated downregulation of HK2 would attenuate the Warburg effect, reduce lactate accumulation, and thereby alleviate the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Consequently, this metabolic rewiring could restore sensitivity to therapies like sorafenib. Our hypothesis provides a novel intersection of metabolic intervention, ncRNA regulation, and therapeutic responsiveness in HCC.
